What they target, given that `compressed_rule_extension` only adds a rule-size power to the previous incumbent (about 0.976 at its best fit, so almost no change):

| Statistic | Observed | What it probes |
|---|---|---|
| `opp_parity_just_outside_yes` | 0.444 | In sets whose examples all share a parity, the yes-rate for opposite-parity targets 1–3 past the edge of the examples' range. Earlier fits suggested the model predicts about 0.52 here. |
| `parity_gap_inside_minus_outside` | −0.052 | Whether parity matters less inside the examples' range than outside it: people may fill in gaps by size but extend beyond the range by parity. |
| `cell_unanimity_rate` | 0.370 | The share of (set, target) pairs, each with about 5 answers, where everyone gave the same answer. If people agree more than the model predicts, its probabilities are too hedged. |
| `set_size_near_outside_gap` | 0.194 | Whether 3–4 examples narrow generalization just outside the range more than 2 examples do, beyond what the size principle predicts. |
| `trial_index_yes_corr` | 0.022 | Drift in yes-rate over the session, which the model has no way to produce. |
| `singleton_far_yes` | 0.339 | How far people generalize from a single example (targets more than 20 away). |
| `nonparity_rule_far_gap` | 0.378 | For targets more than 10 outside the range, the yes-rate when the target shares a specific non-parity rule with all the examples (multiple of 3–12, same last digit, contains a digit, prime, square, cube) minus the yes-rate when it shares none. |
| `below_asym_min_first` | 0.094 | Whether showing the smallest example first holds back extension below it. This is a cue the model ignores. |

None of these repeats a statistic from the iter_0 or iter_1 critiques. The one hit from iter_1 (people use parity beyond the examples' range more than the model does) is now split into the two more specific parity checks at the top of the table. I also saved a memory note listing this round's statistics so later rounds don't propose them again.
